name: authservice
oneLiner: A standalone authentication microservice for ASP.NET Core — and the only finished extraction in the whole portfolio.
summary: Accounts, sign-in, address verification, password reset, TOTP with backup codes, JWT issuance with rotated refresh tokens held as hashes. Google and GitHub sign-in, multi-tenant organisations with roles and invitations, an admin API, an append-only audit log, versioned terms consent and GDPR-compliant data export. It began as a **module lifted out of a private monorepo**, and `EXTRACTION.md` lists exactly what was kept and what was thrown out on purpose. The repository deliberately does not host a canonical instance of its own: it publishes an image to {{term:ghcr}}, and every consumer runs its own instance with its own database and its own signing key. **One codebase, N independent instances, no shared root of trust** — and that is precisely the pattern the rest of the consolidation is meant to repeat.
tests: About 67 executed cases in a single project (61 [Fact] + 2 [Theory] with 6 rows), 1,439 lines. The integration tests boot the whole application on in-memory SQLite — the entire HTTP path with no Docker and no network.
ci: Five workflows: build+test, formatting check, a check that migrations match the model, image build with a smoke test; CodeQL with the security-and-quality suite and a weekly cron; gitleaks over the **full history**; multi-arch image publication on a `v*` tag; GitHub Pages.

docs.label: Notes from the extraction out of the monorepo

components.name: JwtSigningKeys
components.description: Resolves the key material once, at startup, and validates it. The list of **signing keys and the list of validating keys are deliberately different**, which allows a key to be rotated without invalidating tokens already issued. It knows no domain type.

components.name: MigrationBackgroundService + DatabaseReadyHealthCheck
components.description: Schema initialisation after the HTTP server is already listening, with retries. The completion signal drives the readiness endpoint, which returns 503 until the schema is ready. The 'liveness immediately, readiness after the schema' pattern is neutral — and it has been copied into four other repositories.

components.name: AuditService
components.description: An append-only log. Writes are best-effort from the caller's point of view — a failed audit write does not turn a successful operation into a failed one — apart from the method that attaches a row to the unit of work, so that an action and its trace commit together.

components.name: Integration tests on in-memory SQLite
components.description: The factory brings up the real application with the database provider swapped. The entire HTTP path tested with no Docker and no network — a pattern to copy into any ASP.NET Core service.

components.name: TokenService
components.description: Refresh tokens held as hashes, tied into a family; presenting an already-rotated token again invalidates the **whole family** and writes an audit event.

components.name: ProviderEmailVerifier
components.description: Closes the account-takeover path through OAuth: it requires the provider itself to have confirmed the address before it is used to link an account. An unknown provider is treated as unverified by default.

overlaps.reason: Cited there forty times; its extraction pattern is described as a proposed standard with an explicit note that it has one data point — this one.
Consumes the image at v0.3.1 with no source dependency at all — evidence that the pattern works.
Every API validates tokens against this service's JWKS; the service itself is not built there.
Has its own `auto-veritas-authservice` application based on the same image.

product: There is no buyer in the paying sense, and the ADR flatly refuses to compete with Keycloak or Ory on feature count. The real audience is a .NET team that needs a sign-in service of its own and wants to **read it in one afternoon** rather than stand up Keycloak. The portfolio value here is the highest of the lot, though: it is the most engineering-complete security artefact in the whole set, with documentation that records the rejected alternatives.
highlights: Under HS256 the JWKS endpoint returns an **empty set, not a 404** — the consumer gets 'I have no key for you' rather than 'I do not support JWKS'. That is one line that saves someone an hour of diagnosis.
Refresh token reuse detection: the whole family is invalidated plus an audit entry. This is the thing most hand-written identity services do not have.
The image smoke test checks that a container **without a connection string fails and names the missing setting**. It verifies the error message, not only the happy path.
Gitleaks runs over the full history, not over the diff — the only version of that check that means anything in a repository extracted from a monorepo.
A register of six dated deviations and a separate list of closed ones: the project writes down its own weaknesses rather than keeping quiet about them.
gaps: **No committed EF Core migrations.** Both migration projects contain nothing but a project file, and the CI job meant to police this is therefore without effect. The default mode creates the schema and never updates it — so a deployment with a new column will fail at run time.

No tag at all, so the image `ghcr.io/konradcinkusz/authservice:v0.1.0`, given in the README as ready to pin, has probably **never been published** — even though six other repositories already pin it in their configuration.
SQL Server support is declared and untested; the deviations register itself calls this a promise with nothing behind it.
No OTLP telemetry — observability is a console logger plus the service's own audit log.
`Program.cs` is 530 lines and concentrates the whole application composition; the register flags it for refactoring.
next: **Generate and commit migrations** for both providers and switch the recommended mode to migrations. That turns the CI job from an apparent check into a real one.
Push a tag and confirm that the image actually reached GHCR and that the package is public. Six repositories already pin it — today they pin a promise.
Settle the SQL Server deviation: either integration tests, or drop the provider and halve the migration surface.
Fix the copyright line in LICENSE — it carries someone else's name, exactly as in two other repositories.
risks: `docker-compose.yml` contains a plaintext signing secret and an administrator account password. They are described as demonstration-only, but these are ready-to-copy credentials **in the repository of an identity service** — that is, exactly where they cost the most.
The documentation promises an image at a specific version whose existence cannot be confirmed from the repository.
The name `authservice` is entirely generic — a collision in the registry and in search is close to certain.
The `iss` claim is a bare string rather than a URL, which departs from OIDC convention. Deliberate and documented, but it will complicate integration with a client that enforces it.
headline: The pattern that worked — repeat it for K1, but release a tag first
